message: lanes M2: springs and the batched kernels (transform_points, tweens with easing) built, tested and measured.

check.name: batched kernels against glam and plain loops

title: Springs: one transition matrix per preset, one closed form for every regime
body: The spring's motion is linear in (x = position - target, v): [x', v'] = M(dt) [x, v] with M = e^(-at) [[c + a s, s], [-w0^2 s, c - a s]], a = zeta w0, and c, s = cos(wt), sin(wt)/w under-damped or cosh, sinh/w over-damped (w^2 = |a^2 - w0^2|); within |q t^2| < 1e-2 of critical damping their Taylor series (five terms, error below 3e-13), so nothing divides by a vanishing w and zeta = 1 is continuous. Checked against the ODE by RK4 for zeta 0 to 4 (1e-9), the critically damped and undamped closed forms (1e-14), and composition (fifty 10 ms steps equal one 0.5 s step to 1e-13): exact for any dt. Springs keeps lanes as columns with a config index into a deduplicated preset table; step() computes each preset's M once (the transcendentals), then every lane is two multiply-adds per coordinate. Measured (bench/geometry, 10k lanes on 4 presets, f32, results identical): 11.0 us against 59 us for a loop computing each lane's own transition, 5.3-5.5x. Retargeting keeps position and velocity (x is taken from the target each step); a moving lane inside the rest tolerances is snapped, stopped and listed in settled() for that step, and set_target / push_velocity / jump wake it. Lanes are 1-D (a 2-D spring is two lanes): the same M serves every coordinate. Parameterized by (omega, zeta), with from_response (SwiftUI / Framer) and from_physical (stiffness, damping, mass), as parda's graft asked. step never allocates (tests/no_alloc.rs).

title: transform_points in columns; Tweens at parity, a convenience
body: transform_points takes a homography and the points as separate x and y columns, in place, so the projective divide vectorizes: 10k f32 points in 3.4-3.6 us against 4.1-4.2 us for glam's Mat3 * Vec3 and divide per Vec2, 1.17-1.20x (both copy their inputs first; agreement 7e-8). Ease covers the usual named curves (quad, cubic, expo; in, out, in-out) and CSS cubic-bezier, solved by Newton from x with bisection where the slope is too flat (tested against 50-digit mpmath values to 1e-13, and curves with flat ends). Tweens keeps lanes as columns with a rate (1 / duration) instead of the duration, and reports finished lanes. It measures level with a plain loop of Ease::apply over the same lanes (0.99-1.00x): the cost is the curves themselves, so batching tweens buys convenience (finish reporting, retarget from the current value), not speed. Grouping lanes by curve to vectorize the polynomial ones was not tried: worth it only if tween counts reach the tens of thousands per frame.

title: Indexed columns cost a batched loop 8%
body: Tweens::sample first indexed its seven columns by lane (self.from[i], self.to[i], ...): 0.89-0.93x a plain loop over one array of tuples doing the same work, since every index is bounds-checked (the compiler can't know the columns are equally long). Storing 1 / duration instead of the duration (a multiply for a divide) gained little; zipping the columns' iterators (no bounds checks) brought it to 0.99-1.00x. Lesson: in a structure-of-arrays kernel, iterate the columns zipped, never index them, and measure against the plain loop before calling it a batched kernel.
